text: ReDoS (CWE-1333): an attacker-controlled JSON string value flows into a regex with a nested quantifier. In `json2html`, line 40 evaluates `options.withLinks && isUrl(json)` (withLinks defaults to TRUE per `Object.assign` at line 111-115), calling `isUrl(json)` -> `isUrl` (line 20) executes `urlRegexp.test(string)` at line 22 where `urlRegexp = /^(https?:\/\/|ftps?:\/\/)?([a-z0-9%-]+\.){1,}([a-z0-9-]+)?(:(\d{1,5}))?(\/([a-z0-9\-._~:/?#[\]@!$&'()*+,;=%]+)?)?$/i`. The group `([a-z0-9%-]+\.){1,}` is a quantified group containing a quantifier, and the trailing optional host/port/path groups (whose path class includes `.` and `/`) make the host/path split ambiguous, so a long non-matching string forces heavy backtracking and hangs the rendering thread. The `test` call carries a FLOWS_TO self-loop (its own argument is already tainted), reachable_from_entry=true, hop_distance=1, and the highest centrality of any call on this path (0.00103) -- every rendered string value funnels through it.

text: Attacker-controlled JSON string value is interpolated into an `href` attribute and emitted into the DOM: at line 41 `html += '' + json + ''`, taken when `options.withLinks && isUrl(json)` (withLinks defaults to true). The value reaches `$(this).html(html)` at line 128. Attribute-quote breakout is mitigated because the line-33 replace chain already converted `"`->`"` and `'`->`'` BEFORE this concatenation, and `isUrl`'s anchored regex restricts the scheme to http/https/ftp/ftps or none -- so this is NOT a straightforward script-injection. It remains a candidate lead for (a) unvalidated/relative-URL link injection, since the scheme group is optional so a bare host like `evil.com` is emitted as a relative href, and (b) reverse tabnabbing: `target="_blank"` is set with no `rel="noopener noreferrer"`. A verifier should attempt a scheme bypass against the exact regex before accepting any XSS claim here.

text: MISSING rel="noopener noreferrer" ON target="_blank" LINK. At line 41 json2html builds an outbound anchor from JSON-supplied data: `html += '' + json + ''`. The link opens a new browsing context chosen by the (untrusted) JSON author but carries no `rel` attribute at all -- the link-hardening control is entirely absent from the scan. Consequences: (a) the full URL of the embedding page is leaked to the attacker-chosen third-party origin via the Referer header (no `noreferrer`), and (b) on browsers that do not apply the modern implicit-noopener default, the opened document receives a live `window.opener` handle and can navigate the viewer page (reverse tabnabbing). Missing control = `rel="noopener noreferrer"` on the generated target=_blank anchor.

text: NO URL SCHEME ALLOWLIST BEFORE BUILDING href. The only guard on the attacker-supplied value placed into the `href` attribute at line 41 is isUrl() (line 20-22), which is a *shape* regex, not a protocol check: `var urlRegexp = /^(https?:\/\/|ftps?:\/\/)?([a-z0-9%-]+\.){1,}([a-z0-9-]+)?(:(\d{1,5}))?(\/([a-z0-9\-._~:\/?#[\]@!$&'()*+,;=%]+)?)?$/i; return urlRegexp.test(string);`. The scheme group is OPTIONAL (trailing `?`), so the function never asserts that the value actually uses a safe protocol -- it only requires a dot-bearing host-like shape. There is no positive http/https allowlist and no dangerous-scheme denylist anywhere in the scan. HONEST CAVEAT for the verifier: I could NOT construct a working `javascript:`/`data:` bypass, because the anchored `([a-z0-9%-]+\.){1,}` segment requires a literal '.' and excludes ':' outside the optional scheme and the `:(\d{1,5})` port, and because line 33 escapes '"' to '"' which blocks attribute breakout. The defensible residual is the absent control itself plus the behaviour that a scheme-less value such as `evil.com/x` is emitted as a relative href. Rank this below the two leads above; it may well be unexploitable as written.

In json2html(), the HTML-escaping protection is applied ONLY to the string-value branch and is absent on the object-key branch, so attacker-controlled JSON object keys reach a jQuery .html() sink unescaped (DOM XSS). At line 32-33 there is an explicitly-labelled protection ('// Escape tags and quotes') that entity-encodes &, <, >, ' and " for string VALUES. The sibling object branch at lines 80-86 builds `var keyRepr = options.withQuotes ? '"' + key + '"' : key;` and then `html += '' + keyRepr + ''` (line 84) / `html += keyRepr` (line 86) with the raw `key` -- no escape is applied anywhere on that path. The resulting `html` flows into `$(this).html(html)` at line 128. Because `withQuotes` defaults to false (line 114), the default path is line 86, which injects the raw key directly. The protection exists in the same function but was never factored into a shared helper (no htmlEscape/sanitize method exists in the file), so the key path bypasses it entirely. Re-derive: render `$('#x').jsonViewer({'': 1})`.

text: Outdated / end-of-life development toolchain declared as third-party components (components-with-known-vulnerabilities class, no request flow required): eslint@^7.28.0, eslint-plugin-jest@^24.3.6, and jest@^27.0.4. All three are several major versions behind current and the ESLint 7.x and Jest 27.x lines are no longer maintained upstream, so any security fix published for them will never be backported. Risk is bounded: these are build/test tooling rather than code shipped to the browser, and the :Dependency nodes carry NO dev/prod scope property (verified - properties(d) returns only {name, version, scan_id}), so the verifier should read package.json directly to confirm they sit under devDependencies and are therefore not part of the runtime attack surface. The exploitation path for EOL dev tooling is supply-chain / malicious-repo (e.g. a hostile config or plugin executed at lint/test time), not attacker request traffic.

text: jquery@^3.6.0 is the only runtime third-party component declared, and the caret range permits any 3.x up to <4.0.0, so the resolved version is whatever 3.7.x is current at install time rather than a pinned, audited build. This is reported as a low-confidence due-diligence item, NOT as a known-vulnerable component: I want to be explicit that I am NOT asserting a jQuery CVE here, because the well-known jQuery cross-site-scripting advisories (the htmlPrefix/self-closing-tag issues commonly cited as CVE-2020-11022 and CVE-2020-11023) were remediated in jQuery 3.5.0, which 3.6.0 already postdates. The verifier should (a) confirm against a live advisory database whether any advisory applies to the version that actually resolves from `^3.6.0`, and (b) note that the unpinned caret range itself is the weaker finding - an unpinned transitive range means the audited version and the installed version can diverge. The scan graph carries no advisory data, so no vulnerability claim can be grounded from it.
